qt: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

A report published by the Association for Competitive Technology (ACT) in September 2026 raises concerns about the impact of the Digital Markets Act1 (DMA) on European small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), app developers and start-ups. More than two years after the DMA obligations entered into force, ACT argues that the legislation has yet to provide any measurable benefits for smaller businesses. According to the association, regulatory uncertainty surrounding interoperability requirements has contributed to delays in launching innovative technologies, including certain artificial intelligence features, within the EU. The report also highlights growing fragmentation in app distribution and concerns that restrictions on major digital platforms could inadvertently weaken competition for developers and increase operational complexity for SMEs. These findings contrast with the Commission’s April 2026 evaluation, which concluded that the DMA remains fit for purpose and has created new opportunities for businesses and developers. Considering these contrasting assessments, how does the Commission intend to objectively measure the DMA’s impact on SME competitiveness and innovation, address potential unintended consequences, and ensure that the DMA’s implementation supports rather than hinders the EU’s digital development?

Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector and amending Directives (EU) 2019/1937 and (EU) 2020/1828 (OJ L 265, 12.10.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.11.2026) The Association for Competitive Technology (ACT) is largely funded by companies designated as gatekeepers under the Digital Markets Act (DMA)1. Contrary to the ACT’s report, only seven large digital companies have been designated as gatekeepers, and the application of the DMA to these companies is already delivering value to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). For instance, thanks to the interoperability requirement in the DMA, providers of connected devices (e.g. smartwatches) can now interoperate with several Apple iOS features. Today, more than 60 companies, including SMEs, are taking advantage of this result to offer better integrated products to European users. Similarly, every 10 seconds, an EU user picks Firefox over gatekeepers’ browsers through a DMA choice screen. Nothing in the DMA prohibits designated gatekeepers from introducing new products and services in the EU that are compliant with EU law. The decision on whether to roll out their products and services is theirs only. The Commission’s DMA decisions are based on extensive evidence that is carefully assessed. The decisions are taken in full alignment with the DMA’s objectives of promoting contestability and fairness in the digital sector, thereby offering opportunities to innovative SMEs. The Commission is legally required to evaluate the impact of the DMA every three years, with a first review published in April 20262. Based on data and over 400 stakeholders contributions, the review concluded that after two years of enforcement, the DMA has begun to deliver meaningful changes to SMEs and the EU’s digital economy3. At the same time, the report acknowledges the need to continue monitoring any potential unintended consequences and to focus on cloud services and AI.
